In the context of contextual bandits, a well-known issue arises when the reward function is estimated using maximum likelihood estimation, which can lead to biased results due to sampling biases. This problem is particularly pronounced in online settings, where the sampling bias is directly linked to the policy being optimized. We propose a new approach, the Incentive-Biased Maximum Likelihood Estimator (IBMLE), which addresses this issue by incorporating a biasing function that takes into account the policy being optimized. We demonstrate that the IBMLE can be viewed as a modified maximum likelihood estimation problem with a weighted sampling scheme, and derive a closed-form expression for the optimal weights. We also show that the IBMLE can be approximated using a neural network, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a range of contextual bandit settings, including linear and neural networks. Our results indicate that the IBMLE outperforms maximum likelihood estimation, particularly in online settings, and can be used to estimate a range of reward functions, including linear and non-linear models. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of the IBMLE in a range of applications, including recommendation systems and online advertising. Our work provides a new approach to addressing the issue of sampling bias in online settings, and demonstrates the importance of accounting for sampling bias in reward function estimation. We believe that the IBMLE will be a valuable tool for researchers working in online learning and contextual bandits. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of the IBMLE using PyTorch, which can be used to replicate our results. The code is available at https://github.com/berndbischop/ibmle. Botnets, consisting of networks of compromised devices, engage in malicious activities such as spreading malware, launching DDoS attacks, and conducting phishing scams. These botnets often operate through coordinated command and control (C2) systems that issue commands to individual bot members. However, identifying botnets and their associated devices can be challenging due to their ability to disguise themselves and evade detection. This research employs honeypot data to identify botnet groups by analyzing patterns in their commands and comparing them to known C2 servers. By analyzing honeypot logs from multiple servers, we can create a database of command patterns and use this knowledge to detect potential botnets. This approach has been applied to a large dataset of honeypot logs from a major European ISP, resulting in the detection of over 1,000 botnet groups. Our findings indicate that botnet devices often exhibit distinct command patterns, and we have developed a method to identify these groups using natural language processing techniques. This approach has been successfully applied to a real-world dataset, and we have made our code and data available to facilitate further research in this area. Our research has significant implications for the development of effective botnet detection systems, particularly in the context of large-scale honeypot deployments. The goal of entity linking is to identify and connect specific references within text to a vast database of entities. This complex task is often divided into two main categories: general entity linking and named entity recognition. However, we propose a more detailed approach by categorizing entities into 12 groups, including locations, people, organizations, and more. This entity linking task, known as comprehensive entity linking, is particularly challenging in unstructured Wikipedia content. To address this, we have developed WikiGUM, a comprehensive entity linking dataset that includes 12 categories and over 1.5 million Wikipedia articles. WikiGUM is designed to evaluate the performance of comprehensive entity linking systems, which we have tested using a state-of-the-art model. The results show that our model performs well on most categories, but there is still room for improvement in certain areas, such as categorization and linking to concepts. To facilitate further research, we have made WikiGUM available for public use. This process continues until a satisfying assignment is found or a user-defined timeout is reached. The resulting circuit can then be optimized for speed using traditional techniques. This paper introduces a pioneering 3D object detection method that leverages
multiple perspectives. To begin, we create a comprehensive, voxel-based 3D
framework that can efficiently process images from various angles. Next, we
develop a novel approach to aggregating object features across different views,
utilizing a unique combination of spatial and spatial-temporal information.
Our innovative technique involves establishing connections between objects
seen in the same scene and then identifying correlations among corresponding
features in different images. This allows our model to capture the underlying
relationships between objects across views. To further enhance performance, we
introduce a new loss function that encourages objects detected in different
images to have similar characteristics. Our approach was extensively tested on the
NuScenes benchmark, where it achieved exceptional results, surpassing the
previous state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieved an impressive 71.7%
AP50, 83.8% AP75, and 0.876 AMOTA. Our code and pre-trained models are
available for public access at https://github.com/autonomousvision/3DAggregation.

the creation of the NuScenes dataset. Lastly, we would like to extend our

This paper introduces a novel theory called Resilient Limit Assessment (RLA), 
enabling the computation of worst-case limit loads under various uncertainty conditions.
The RLA method is founded on the concept of resilience, which describes the 
tendency of a structural system to withstand degradation in response to external 
forces and random factors. By leveraging the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and 
the RLA formulation, the proposed approach can efficiently determine the worst-case 
limit loads, even in complex scenarios involving multiple random variables. 
Theoretical derivations and numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of 
RLA in computing resilient limit loads, which serve as a lower bound for worst-case 
limit loads, across different structural systems and uncertainty conditions. 
Furthermore, the proposed approach can be adapted to other limit states, such as 
stresses and deformations, to provide a comprehensive understanding of a 
structural system's resilience in various loading scenarios. The RLA method is 
expected to facilitate the design of robust structures capable of withstanding 
unpredictable and adverse environmental conditions. The RLA formulation can be 
applied to a wide range of problems, including structural systems with random 
material properties, geometric uncertainties, and other types of uncertainties. 
The proposed approach can also be extended to other fields, such as robust design, 
safety assessment, and reliability analysis. The RLA method is anticipated to serve 
as a valuable tool for structural optimization and robust design in various 
engineering applications. The proposed approach can be implemented using 
conventional optimization algorithms, such as the Sequential Quadratic Programming 
(SQP) method, to efficiently solve the associated optimization problems. 
Theoretical and numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the RLA method 
in computing resilient limit loads, even in complex scenarios involving multiple 
random variables. The proposed approach can be applied to a wide range of

This research introduces a new family of Krylov solvers designed for systems
with a specific saddle-point structure, where the matrix $A$ is negative definite
and $S$ is positive definite. These solvers can efficiently handle systems
where $A$ is singular, a common scenario in many optimization problems. We
propose a new approach that combines a regularization term with $A$ to ensure
invertibility and develops solvers that leverage this modified matrix. We
evaluate the effectiveness of our solvers on a range of large-scale test
problems, comparing them to established methods like MINRES-DR and GMRES-DR. The
results show that our solvers can outperform these alternatives on certain
problems, particularly those with highly ill-conditioned matrices. Furthermore,
we demonstrate that our solvers can be enhanced with a range of preconditioning
techniques, including incomplete factorization and classical iterative methods. 
These enhancements can significantly improve performance on large-scale problems,
with some configurations leading to speedups of up to 2.5 times over the
unpreconditioned solvers. Overall, our research highlights the potential of
saddle-position solvers in tackling complex optimization problems, particularly
in cases where traditional methods fall short. The code developed in this research
is available for public use.  https://github.com/UMN-Numerical-Analysis/SPKrylov.git.

In ensemble Q-learning, a diverse set of Q-networks is trained to mitigate the impact of individual network weaknesses. The proposed method is evaluated in the context of deep Q-learning and Atari 2000 games, demonstrating that it enhances representation variety without compromising performance. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis is provided to explain the relationship between representation variety and ensemble Q-learning's effectiveness. In recent years, the use of deep learning models has become widespread in various industries, but the potential risks associated with sensitive data have led to growing concerns about data privacy. To mitigate these risks, data anonymization techniques are being explored to protect sensitive information while preserving data utility. Despite the development of anonymization methods, the existing approaches often fall short in effectively safeguarding against sophisticated attacks that utilize background knowledge. To address this issue, we introduce a novel data type-conscious anonymization method that leverages the Ambiguity-Autoencoder to safeguard both data privacy and utility. Our approach, Ambiguity-Ambiguous Autoencoder (A2A), employs a unique Ambiguity-Ambiguous mechanism to generate multiple plausible data types, thereby enhancing data privacy and providing a safeguard against attacks. Furthermore, the Ambiguous mechanism is designed to minimize the loss of data utility by introducing minimal distortion. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of A2A in safeguarding sensitive information and preserving data utility across various datasets. Notably, the Ambiguous mechanism outperforms existing anonymization methods in terms of data privacy and utility. Our approach is also adaptable to different data types, including numerical, categorical, and mixed data, and can be easily integrated into existing deep learning models to safeguard sensitive information. The effectiveness of word embedding techniques in capturing semantic relationships among words has been well-documented, with applications extending to tasks such as identifying semantic similarities and analogies.  Despite the growing interest in utilizing word embeddings for various natural language processing tasks, there remains a lack of standardized benchmark datasets specifically tailored for evaluating their performance in languages other than English.  In an effort to address this gap, we introduce three benchmark datasets for the Tatar language, which include similarity pairs, semantic parallelisms, and related words, with accompanying English translations.  The proposed datasets are designed to facilitate the assessment of word embeddings in languages other than English, with a particular focus on the Tatar language, which is a member of the Turkic language family.  To validate the utility of these datasets, we conducted an evaluation of word embeddings generated using the FastText and GloVe algorithms, with a comparative analysis of their performance in English and Tatar.  The results of our study indicate that word embeddings generated using the GloVe algorithm exhibit superior performance in capturing semantic relationships among words in both English and Tatar.  Furthermore, our analysis reveals that word embeddings generated using the FastText algorithm exhibit a higher degree of accuracy in identifying related words in English, whereas in Tatar, both the GloVe and FastText algorithms demonstrate comparable performance in this regard. Recent advancements in medical image segmentation have been driven by the emergence of transformer-based models, which excel at capturing long-range dependencies within images. However, the reliance on self-attention mechanisms in these models can lead to an uneven distribution of computational power, with a focus on prominent features while neglecting others. This issue is particularly pronounced in medical images, where subtle details are often crucial for accurate segmentation. To address this challenge, we introduce the Dual Attention-directed Effective Transformer (DAE-Former), a novel architecture that leverages two attention mechanisms to dynamically allocate computational resources. By combining a spatial attention mechanism with a channel attention mechanism, DAE-Former can effectively focus on the most informative features within images. Our proposed model is evaluated on three prominent medical segmentation datasets, demonstrating its ability to achieve state-of-the-art performance while reducing computational complexity. Notably, DAE-Former outperforms existing methods by a significant margin, with a 2.5% improvement in Dice score on the MS-CMR Segmentation dataset. These attacks, known as backdoor attacks, involve training neural networks to recognize patterns that are not inherently present in the data. When a malicious trigger is introduced during the training process, the network can be triggered to produce incorrect results under specific conditions. In this study, we investigate the vulnerability of face recognition models to such attacks and propose a novel defense mechanism that can detect and prevent malicious triggers from affecting face recognition accuracy. Our proposed method is also efficient, with a computational cost of only 0.01 seconds per image. We believe that this study will contribute to the development of more robust and secure face recognition systems that can withstand malicious attacks. This research introduces a novel approach to point cloud resampling, focusing on preserving the structure of the input data, which is represented by a hypergraph. Each vertex in the hypergraph represents a data point, and the corresponding edges connect subsets of vertices that belong to the same resampling group. By iteratively refining the hypergraph, the proposed method achieves high resampling efficiency. Specifically, in each refinement step, the hypergraph is converted into a traditional graph, and a modified PageRank algorithm is applied to identify the most critical vertex in each group. This process is repeated until the desired resampling rate is reached. To further enhance resilience, the proposed method incorporates a data-driven strategy that dynamically adjusts the resampling rate based on the confidence level of the hypergraph. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this approach compared to existing resampling methods. Current language check tools are limited in their ability to accurately assess the impact of grammatical errors on a sentence's meaning, often failing to prioritize more severe mistakes or overlooking lesser ones entirely. To address this shortfall, we introduce a new method for evaluating grammatical error significance, based on a dataset of annotated errors developed in conjunction with a human-provided reference. This approach is then applied to a large corpus of English translations from a popular language learning platform, revealing a notable disparity between the frequency of corrections provided by the language check tool and the significance of those errors as determined by our method, which suggests that the tool is more effective at identifying minor errors than more substantial ones. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the language check tool's performance and the linguistic characteristics of the sentences it processes. These obstacles stem from the muons' short lifetimes and the muon cataphoric condition, which necessitates a long, curved beamline. We will examine the various collider designs that have been proposed, highlighting their advantages and drawbacks. We will also discuss the advancements made in muon production, storage, and catalysis, as well as the current state of beam dynamics, luminosity, and cost estimation. Furthermore, we will touch on the key issues that need to be resolved before a muon collider can be constructed. This presentation is based on a talk delivered at the Snowmass 2021 Collider Frontier Workshop.

A dead pixel is an irregular component within an image sensor that captures light and converts it into an electrical signal, resulting in distorted images. This dead pixel anomaly is characterized by a dark spot or ring in affected images. This study presents a novel method for detecting dead pixels in image sensors, utilizing a deep learning approach that leverages a convolutional neural network. The proposed model incorporates a unique efficient receptive field (ERF) module, a type of convolutional block that incorporates a dilated convolutional layer to amplify the field of view. This design enables the model to capture broader contextual information while minimizing the number of parameters required, thus enhancing its computational efficiency. The proposed model was evaluated on the K210 dead pixel dataset and demonstrated superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 0.98 AUC score. The proposed model's efficiency is further highlighted by its ability to run on the low-power, open-source Movidius Myriad X neural processor. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are increasingly being used in various applications such as autonomous vehicles, augmented reality, and robotics. However, the high computational demands of DNNs pose a significant challenge, particularly in resource-constrained edge devices. To address this issue, researchers have proposed a range of solutions, including the use of model compression and distributed inference across edge and cloud environments. This paper presents AppealNet, a highly efficient edge/cloud collaborative architecture for DNN inference that leverages both edge-based and cloud-based resources. AppealNet's edge-based inference module is designed to handle a subset of the DNN's layers, while the cloud-based module handles the remaining layers. By carefully selecting the layers to be executed on the edge, AppealNet can minimize communication overhead and reduce inference latency. The proposed architecture is evaluated on a range of DNNs, including ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and Inception-ResNet-v4, using a Raspberry Pi 4B as the edge device and a Google Cloud instance as the cloud-based module. The results demonstrate that AppealNet can achieve significant reductions in inference latency, including a 2.5x improvement over the cloud-based approach and a 1.5x improvement over the edge-based approach. AppealNet's accuracy is also comparable to that of the baseline approaches, with a 0.5% top-1 error rate on the ImageNet validation set. The proposed architecture is highly versatile and can be easily adapted to a range of edge/cloud inference scenarios. AppealNet's source code is available on GitHub. The authors plan to continue their work on the AppealNet architecture and explore its potential applications in real-time inference scenarios. The FAccT conference has been a leading platform for the presentation of research in fairness, accountability, and ethics in data science and technology since 2015. This comprehensive examination, encompassing both quantitative and qualitative analyses, reviews the past four years of FAccT, focusing on research areas, publication trends, and the conference's impact on academic and practical fields. Key findings include a notable increase in diversity among research topics, a shift towards more practical applications, and a growing presence of industry professionals. However, the review also highlights several concerns, such as a lack of engagement from underrepresented groups, insufficient representation of industry in terms of hiring practices, and the conference's environmental footprint. Ultimately, the analysis identifies avenues for FAccT to enhance its reach and effectiveness in fostering positive change in data and technology. This research serves as a foundation for FAccT's future development and the data science community's efforts to create a more responsible and equitable field.

We introduce TIPS, a text-aided pose generation framework capable of producing a pose from a text description and an image. Unlike conventional methods that utilize text to refine errors in an image's pose annotation, TIPS generates a pose from a text description without relying on existing image data. To accomplish this, TIPS employs a two-part approach, where a text-driven pose generator creates a pose from a text description, and a pose transformer refines the generated pose to align with the image content. In the realm of active learning, researchers have been exploring the benefits of guiding the selection of query examples for model training. Conversely, this work aims to enhance active learning by improving the quality of the model, specifically by enhancing its performance on the available labeled data. Furthermore, Advise's ability to identify and correct model errors is validated through a qualitative analysis. Overall, the results demonstrate Advise's potential to significantly enhance active learning by improving the quality of the model. To mitigate this issue, we propose a regularization approach that incorporates a penalty term to reduce the reward function estimation errors. Our experiments demonstrate that this regularization method effectively alleviates the misalignment problem and enhances the task robustness. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the impact of reward function estimation errors on the task performance and misalignment, and offers a practical solution to address this issue. Our approach, Self-Managed IoT, utilizes a personalized, decentralized architecture that prioritizes user trust and device relationships.  By leveraging social network information, SMSI can efficiently offload computations, achieving a balance between quality of service and user trust.  Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SMSI in achieving high system utilization, low latency, and user satisfaction.  Furthermore, SMSI's ability to manage personal data and computations on the edge provides users with greater transparency and control over their information.  Our findings also highlight the importance of considering user trust and device relationships in IoT architecture design.  By empowering users to manage their personal data, SMSI sets a new standard for IoT systems, enabling a more decentralized and user-centric approach to edge computing. domination phase during inflation. Additionally, we examine the potential of
gravitational wave detectors to observe these signals, and find that the
detection of these signals may be feasible in the future. Finally, we discuss
the implications of these findings for our understanding of the early universe.

Deep learning models have been found to perpetuate biases in their predictions, often due to biased training data. To address this issue, researchers have developed methods for creating fair representations, which aim to eliminate these biases. However, these methods often require access to sensitive information such as protected class labels, making them impractical in real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, we propose a self-supervised approach that learns fair representations without relying on such sensitive information. Our method, which we call Adversarial Acquired Fair Representations using Dampening and Piling (AADEP), leverages the idea that biased representations are characterized by high variance, while fair representations are represented by low variance. To achieve this, we use a two-step process where we first use a fair representation as a reference point to dampen the variance of biased representations, and then use this reference point to pile the variance of the biased representations, effectively canceling out the biased components. To ensure that our learned representations are indeed fair, we use a discriminator to classify representations into protected classes, and then use adversarial training to ensure that our representations are not distinguishable by the discriminator. Our experiments demonstrate that AADEP achieves state-of-the-art results in fairness while maintaining competitive performance on downstream tasks. Additionally, AADEP is the first self-supervised approach to achieve state-of-the-art fairness while not requiring access to sensitive information. In a multi-armed bandit scenario, we examine a sequence of arms with unique rewards that must be selected in a way that meets specific requirements. The sequence is considered monotone if the rewards of the selected arms increase or remain the same over time. We investigate how to choose such a sequence while minimizing the regret, which is the difference between the rewards obtained from optimal choices and our choices. We have developed a new algorithm that achieves a regret of O(√(m*log(N))) after N arm pulls, where m is the number of unique arms and N is the total number of arms pulled. This algorithm outperforms existing methods, which have a regret of O(√(m*N)) or O(N), by leveraging the monotonicity constraint. We have also extended this approach to a more general scenario where the rewards are non-stationary and the sequence of arms must be chosen based on a given monotone function. The proposed algorithm can be applied to a variety of problems, including the multi-armed bandit demanding monotone arm problem, the demanding monotone arm problem, the demanding monotone arm problem with a fixed arm, and the demanding monotone arm problem with a fixed arm and a time window. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our algorithm through numerical simulations. The source code of our algorithm is available online. resulting in an increased demand for courses and tutorials to educate students

the emergence of various online platforms offering DL courses, workshops, and

propose the development of an open standard, called DLSpec, which enables the 
creation of a unified course catalog. This standard aims to provide a common 
framework for describing DL courses, allowing for the comparison and exchange of 
courses across different platforms. By adopting DLSpec, online platforms can 
integrate course descriptions into a single, standardized database, facilitating 
the discovery and exchange of courses and promoting a more consistent and 
consistent representation of DL courses. To achieve this goal, we have designed a 
minimal and flexible schema for DLSpec, which covers essential aspects of DL 
courses, including their content, structure, and assessment methods. This schema 
can be easily extended to accommodate additional information and is intended to be 
a starting point for further development. By promoting the adoption of DLSpec, we 
aim to simplify the process of creating and sharing DL courses, ultimately leading 
to a more cohesive and collaborative community. To facilitate this goal, we have 
made DLSpec available as an open specification and encourage developers to 
contribute their feedback and suggestions. This paper provides a detailed overview of 
DLSpec, its schema, and its potential applications, along with a discussion of its 
implications and limitations. We also highlight the potential benefits of DLSpec 
for DL course providers and platform operators. Finally, we outline future research

This research focuses on the theoretical foundations of the Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm, particularly its ability to achieve first-order convergence in population-based optimization problems. Building on the log-concave probability framework, we expand our understanding to include non-log-concave distributions. To address this, we introduce a novel concept of "weak" non-log-concavity, which is accompanied by a key property: the existence of a convex function that serves as a tight bound for a specific population objective function. Leveraging this insight, we establish a first-order convergence result for the Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm, which is contingent upon the algorithm's step size being sufficiently small. Moreover, we demonstrate that this convergence rate is characterized by a polynomial time dependency on the problem dimension. To illustrate the practical implications of our findings, we provide a convergence analysis for a specific optimization problem, which is defined by a non-log-concave probability distribution. This analysis is accompanied by numerical experiments that validate our theoretical predictions. Ultimately, our research paves the way for the development of novel sampling strategies for non-log-concave probability distributions. To facilitate further research in this area, we provide a comprehensive appendix that outlines the theoretical foundations of the Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm, including its convergence properties. This appendix is intended to serve as a self-contained resource that can be studied independently. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of HSC4D in accurately reconstructing 4D scenes in various environments. This research has the potential to significantly impact fields such as robotics, AR/VR, and location-based services, by providing a more accurate and human-centric representation of the world. Furthermore, ASL's ability to adapt to various feature representations and classification tasks makes it a versatile solution. The code and pre-trained models for ASL are publicly available for further research and implementation. This method is tested on simulated data and compared to existing methods, showing its effectiveness. This research demonstrates the importance of accounting for temporal correlations in segmenting time series data. A publicly available implementation of the method is provided on GitHub. The first stage utilizes a convolutional neural network to predict occlusion, and the second stage utilizes a differentiable renderer to refine depth estimates, all while incorporating occlusion information.
